title: K Inverse Pairs Array
statement:
In an array `nums`, an *inverse pair* is a pair of indices `(i, j)` with `0 <= i < j < nums.length` whose values are out of order, that is `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

Given integers `n` and `k`, count the arrangements of the numbers `1, 2, ..., n` (each used exactly once) that have exactly `k` inverse pairs. The count can be very large, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `n!` arrangements and counting their inverse pairs only works for tiny `n`. Instead, build arrangements by adding the largest number last. Take any arrangement of `1..i-1` and insert `i`: it is bigger than everything, so it forms an inverse pair with each number placed after it. Putting it at the very end adds `0` pairs, one step to the left adds `1`, and so on up to `i - 1` at the front. Every arrangement of `1..i` is made exactly once this way.

So if `dp[i][j]` counts arrangements of `1..i` with `j` inverse pairs, then `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i-1][j-1] + ... + dp[i-1][j-i+1]` (skipping negative indices). That sum covers a window of `i` consecutive cells in the previous row, so it can slide along with one addition and one subtraction per cell, as with prefix sums.

## Approach

1. `prev` is the row for `i = 1`: the single arrangement `[1]` has `0` pairs, so `prev[0] = 1` and the rest are `0`.
2. For each `i` from `2` to `n`, build `curr` from left to right while keeping `window`, the sum of the last `i` cells of `prev`.
3. At column `j`, add `prev[j]` to `window`; once `j >= i`, subtract `prev[j - i]`, which has slid out. Store `window` in `curr[j]`.
4. Keep every value modulo `10^9 + 7`, adding `MOD` before reducing a subtraction.
5. After the last row, return `prev[k]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, `k = 0`, so each row has only column `0`. Start with `prev = [1]`. For `i = 2`: `window = 0 + 1 = 1`, so `curr = [1]`. For `i = 3`: again `window = 1`, `curr = [1]`. The answer is `1`: only the sorted array `[1,2,3]`. (With `k = 1`, the rows are `[1,0]`, `[1,1]`, `[1,2]`, giving Example 2's `2`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · k): each of the `n` rows fills `k + 1` cells in O(1).
- Space: O(k): only two rows are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Summing the whole window for every cell is O(n · k · n), too slow at the limits; slide it instead.
- After subtracting under a modulus, add `MOD` first or the value can go negative.
- The window is `i` cells wide (insertions add `0` to `i - 1` pairs), so the cell leaving is `prev[j - i]`, not `prev[j - i + 1]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `prev` | counts for arrangements of `1..i-1`, indexed by inverse pairs |
| `curr` | counts for arrangements of `1..i` being built |
| `i` | the number being inserted, the current row |
| `j` | the number of inverse pairs, the current column |
| `window` | sum of `prev[j - i + 1..j]` modulo `MOD` |

narration.3: This row counts arrangements of the numbers 1 to i - 1 by their number of inverse pairs; start with i = 1.
narration.4: The single arrangement [1] has no inverse pairs.
narration.6: Add the numbers 2, 3, ..., n one at a time as the new largest value.
narration.8: The running sum of the cells of the previous row that can reach column j.
narration.9: Fill each possible count of inverse pairs from 0 to k.
narration.10: Inserting i at the very end adds no pairs, so prev[j] enters the window.
narration.11: Once j reaches i, the window holds one cell too many...
narration.12: ...so remove prev[j - i], which would need i new pairs, one more than inserting i can add.
narration.14: The window is exactly the number of arrangements of 1..i with j inverse pairs.
narration.16: The new row becomes the previous row for the next number.
narration.18: After inserting n, the cell for k pairs is the answer.
